title: DIY Spiralizer Cleaning Kit Using Baking Soda and Lemon
meta_description: Stop struggling with stuck-on veggie residue! Learn how to make a DIY spiralizer cleaning kit using lemon and baking soda to keep your blades sharp.
html:
There is nothing quite like the satisfaction of turning a giant zucchini into a mountain of curls for a low-carb pasta night. However, if you’ve used a spiralizer, you know the struggle: those tiny, sharp blades act like magnets for sticky carrot pulp and stubborn potato starch. When those residues dry, they become like concrete, making it dangerous and frustrating to clean.

Instead of scrubbing with a sponge that gets shredded by the blades, I prefer a targeted approach. By putting together a DIY spiralizer cleaning kit using simple pantry staples like baking soda and lemon, you can break down organic matter and sanitize the blades without using harsh chemicals that might linger on your food.

What’s in Your DIY Spiralizer Cleaning Kit?

You don't need a fancy store-bought scrub brush to get your gear sparkling. To build your own kit, gather these few items. The combination of acidity from the lemon and the mild abrasiveness of the baking soda creates a chemical reaction that lifts debris without scratching the stainless steel.

  • Baking Soda: The heavy lifter for scrubbing and neutralizing odors.
  • Fresh Lemons: The citric acid cuts through sticky resins and adds a fresh scent.
  • A Soft-Bristled Toothbrush: Essential for reaching into the tight crevices of the blade housing.
  • Dish Soap: A mild, grease-cutting soap for the final rinse.
  • Microfiber Cloth: To dry the blades immediately and prevent water spots.

Step-by-Step: Cleaning Your Vegetable Spiralizer

Whether you use a handheld model or a larger countertop version, the process is the same. If you're using a Vegetable Spiralizer to make zoodles or carrot noodles, it's best to start this process immediately after you finish prepping your meal.

First, rinse the unit under cool water to remove the bulk of the vegetable fragments. Next, sprinkle a generous amount of baking soda directly onto the blades. While the powder is still dry, slice a lemon in half and use the cut side of the lemon as a "sponge." Rub the lemon directly onto the baking soda-covered blades. You’ll see it fizz—that's the citric acid reacting with the sodium bicarbonate to lift the stuck-on pulp.

Let this paste sit for about five to ten minutes. This "soaking" period is crucial for those stubborn root vegetables like sweet potatoes that leave a starchy film. After the wait, use your toothbrush to gently scrub the areas around the blade edges and the turning mechanism.

Why Baking Soda and Lemon Work Better Than Soap Alone

Most of us reach for a sponge and dish soap first, but soap is designed to break down fats and oils. Vegetable residue—especially from carrots and beets—is more about starches and sugars. These create a biological "glue" that bonds to the metal.

Baking soda is a mild alkali that helps break these bonds. When you add the lemon, you introduce an acid. This duo creates a bubbling action that physically pushes particles away from the surface of the blade. Plus, the lemon acts as a natural disinfectant, ensuring your DIY spiralizer cleaning kit doesn't just make the tool look clean, but actually sanitizes it for the next use.

Maintaining Your Vegetable Spiralizer for Longevity

To keep your Vegetable Spiralizer working efficiently, the goal is to prevent buildup from hardening. If you can't clean it immediately, a quick rinse is better than nothing. However, avoid the temptation to throw your spiralizer in the dishwasher unless the manual explicitly says it's safe.

High heat in dishwashers can sometimes warp the plastic housings of countertop models or dull the precision edges of the blades over time. Hand-washing with your lemon and soda kit keeps the blades sharper for longer, meaning your zucchini noodles will have a clean cut rather than looking mashed or torn.

Safe Storage After Cleaning

The final step of using your DIY spiralizer cleaning kit is the dry-down. Water left on carbon steel or even some stainless steel alloys can lead to spotting or, in extreme cases, oxidation.

Use a clean microfiber cloth to dry every nook and cranny. If you have a countertop model with multiple blade attachments, store them in a dry place, separated by a paper towel or a cloth to prevent the blades from knocking against each other and losing their edge. Once dried and stored, your tool is ready for your next low-carb feast.

FAQ

Can I use vinegar instead of lemon?

Yes, white distilled vinegar works similarly to lemon because it is acidic. However, lemon is generally preferred for food-prep tools because it leaves a pleasant scent and is slightly gentler on the plastic components than concentrated vinegar.

How often should I use the baking soda scrub?

You don't need to use the full kit every single time you make a snack. A standard soap-and-water wash is fine for a few uses. I recommend the baking soda and lemon deep clean once a week, or whenever you notice the blades aren't gliding through the vegetables as smoothly as they used to.

Is it safe to use a scrub brush on the blades?

Avoid using steel wool or coarse scouring pads, as these will scratch the metal and create microscopic grooves where bacteria can hide. Stick to a nylon toothbrush or a soft plastic brush to safely remove debris without damaging the blade's edge.
